I'm working on the Gleam compiler and I'd like to add a new warning for a JavaScript-specific limitation in bit array pattern matching.

*   When compiling for the JavaScript target, if a bit array pattern contains an integer segment with a compile-time literal size greater than 52 bits (expressed either as a bare integer literal or via the size() option), the compiler must emit a warning.

*   The warning title for an oversized JavaScript bit array integer segment must be exactly: 'Truncated bit array segment'.

*   The warning body for an oversized JavaScript bit array integer segment must state the exact bit size and the JavaScript limit: 'This segment is a {N}-bit long integer, but on the JavaScript target numbers have at most 52 bits. It would be truncated to its first 52 bits.' where {N} is replaced with the actual size.

*   The warning hint for an oversized JavaScript bit array integer segment must be exactly: 'Did you mean to use the `bytes` segment option?'

*   The warning must only be emitted when the size is compile-time known and strictly greater than 52. Integer segments with size 52 or below must not trigger this warning.

*   The warning must only be emitted when the pattern segment binds a variable (e.g., `<<n:size(53)>>` or `<<number:123>>`); patterns that do not capture a value in the segment do not require this warning.

*   Existing warning messages for 'todo found', 'panic used as a function', and 'todo used as a function' must not have a blank line between the main warning body text and the 'Hint:' line — the hint must immediately follow the body text.

*   The 'Inefficient use of list.length' warning body text must be formatted as a single reflowed paragraph without a trailing blank line before the hint. The body must read: 'The `list.length` function has to iterate across the whole list to calculate the length, which is wasteful if you only need to know if the list is empty or not.'

This is a **"Truncated bit array segment"** warning that the Gleam compiler emits. The compiler now raises a warning on the JavaScript target when a pattern attempts to extract an int larger than JavaScript supports, to avoid unexpected results.

The exact warning you're referencing looks like this: warning: Truncated bit array segment — "This segment is a 152-bit long int, but on the JavaScript target numbers have at most 52 bits. It would be truncated to its first 52 bits."

## Why This Happens

The root cause is a fundamental limitation of JavaScript's number type. The largest size an int can have on JavaScript is 52 bits, after which precision is lost. This is because JavaScript uses IEEE-754 double-precision floating-point numbers, which can only represent integers exactly up to a certain range.

## How to Fix It

The compiler provides a helpful hint alongside the warning: "Hint: Did you mean to use the `bytes` segment option?"

If you're working with data larger than 52 bits (such as a SHA hash in the example), you likely want to extract it as raw bytes rather than as an integer, since the integer representation would lose precision.

## Related Context

This is part of a broader set of safety features Gleam has added for the JavaScript target. There's a related but distinct warning for integer literals: "Int is outside the safe range on JavaScript... This integer value is too large to be represented accurately by JavaScript's number type. To avoid this warning integer values must be in the range -(2^53 - 1) - (2^53 - 1)."

The compiler also warns about literal truncation in bit array segments. The compiler now raises a warning when it can tell that an int segment with a literal value is going to be truncated. This will help folks understand a behaviour that may be unexpected.

Both features were contributed largely by Giacomo Cavalieri and Richard Viney, and are part of Gleam's ongoing effort to make bit array behavior consistent and predictable across the BEAM (Erlang) and JavaScript targets.

The feature is implemented and verified end-to-end. Here's what I did, all in source files (no `tests/` changes):

## New warning: oversized JavaScript bit array integer segment

**`compiler-core/src/type_/error.rs`** — Added a `JavaScriptBitArrayUnsafeInt { location, size: BigInt }` variant to the `Warning` enum, and wired it into the `location()` accessor.

**`compiler-core/src/ast.rs`** — Added `BitArraySize::compile_time_number() -> Option<BigInt>` (mirrors the existing `non_zero_compile_time_number`, recursing through `Block`).

**`compiler-core/src/type_/pattern.rs`** — Added `check_matched_int_is_in_js_bounds`, called at the end of `infer_pattern_segment`. It emits the warning only when: the target is JavaScript (and not a JS-external function), the segment type is `Int`, the value binds a variable (`Pattern::Variable`/`Pattern::Assign`), and the compile-time-known size (`size × unit`, covering both bare literals and `size()`) is strictly `> 52`.

**`compiler-core/src/warning.rs`** — Rendering with the exact title `Truncated bit array segment`, body `This segment is a {N}-bit long integer, but on the JavaScript target numbers have at most 52 bits. It would be truncated to its first 52 bits.`, and hint `Did you mean to use the \`bytes\` segment option?`.

**`language-server/src/code_action.rs`** — Added the new variant to the exhaustive match (returns `None`).

## Formatting fixes (also in `warning.rs`)
- `Todo`, and the `panic`/`todo` used-as-function hints: changed `\n\n` → `\n` so `Hint:` immediately follows the body.
- `Inefficient use of list.length`: reflowed the body into a single `wrap`-ed paragraph with no trailing blank line before the hint.

## Verified behavior
Compiling a real JS-target project confirmed:
- `<<n:size(53)>>` and `<<number:123>>` → warning ✓
- `<<ok:size(52)>>` (size 52) → no warning ✓
- `<<0:size(60)>>` (no variable bound) → no warning ✓
- Erlang target → no warning ✓
- The three existing warnings render with the hint immediately after the body ✓

Sources: [gleam-lang/gleam PR #3798](https://github.com/gleam-lang/gleam/pull/3798), [Issue #3287](https://github.com/gleam-lang/gleam/issues/3287)
